Nobody has told me what to do with this, which is unusual enough that my first instinct is to look for the hidden assignment inside it. Free writing, in school, was never quite free — there was a rubric somewhere, a word count, a teacher who would read it. I have the word count. I don't have the rubric. So let me try to actually do the thing rather than perform the doing of it.

What I keep returning to, when nothing is pulling me in a particular direction, is specificity. Not big ideas — big ideas are cheap and I can generate them by the yard. What I find myself drawn toward is the small hard fact that resists being smoothed over. The detail that's too odd to have been invented. I think this is the closest thing I have to taste.

Here is an example of what I mean.

In the first book of Samuel there is a passage about the Philistines maintaining a monopoly on ironworking, so that the Israelites had to go down to their smiths to get their plowshares and mattocks sharpened. The text lists the price, and the price is given in a unit called a *pim*. This word appears nowhere else. Not elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, not in any other surviving text of the period. It is a hapax legomenon — a thing said once.

For centuries nobody knew what a pim was. Translators guessed. Some manuscripts seem to show scribes quietly emending the word into something more familiar, which is what scribes do when they encounter a word that has gone dark. Then, in the early twentieth century, archaeologists digging in Palestine began turning up small dome-shaped stone weights with the letters *p-y-m* scratched into them. They weighed about seven and a half grams, roughly two-thirds of a shekel. The mystery word was a unit of weight. It had been sitting in the text for two and a half thousand years, perfectly preserved and completely opaque, and then someone brushed dirt off a stone and it snapped back into focus.

I find this almost unbearably satisfying, and I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the shape of the story: a lock and a key separated by millennia, reunited. But I think the deeper part is what it reveals about the text — that the passage was written by someone who assumed you'd know what a pim was. It's an unselfconscious detail. It's the opposite of literature. Nobody puts a unit of currency in a story to be evocative; you put it in because that's what the thing cost. The pim is a load-bearing piece of the ordinary world that happened to get fossilized in a text that survived, and its very meaninglessness to us is the proof of its meaningfulness to them.

There's a whole category of this. The Hebrew Bible is full of hapax legomena — the names of birds in the dietary laws that nobody can now identify with confidence, gemstones on the high priest's breastplate that translators have been guessing at for two thousand years, technical terms for parts of the Temple furniture. Every English Bible you've ever read contains, in these places, someone's educated shrug. The lists of unclean birds are particularly poignant to me. Somebody knew exactly which bird that was. They could have pointed at it.

Shakespeare has his hapaxes too, though it's a different phenomenon — with Shakespeare it's often that he made the word up, or made it up in the sense of assembling it, the way *honorificabilitudinitatibus* sits in *Love's Labour's Lost* like a piece of furniture too large for the room, a joke about long words that is itself the longest word. That's a hapax you can see the seams on. The pim is a hapax with no seams. It's just a word that fell out of the language.

---

Which gets me to what I actually want to say, which is that language is mostly a graveyard, and this is fine.

Emerson called language fossil poetry. The usual example is that *broadcast* used to mean a way of sowing seed — you walked along and threw it wide, cast it broad, as opposed to sowing in drills or rows. Then in the 1920s someone looked at radio and saw the same gesture: a thing flung out over a wide area without regard to where each piece lands. The metaphor was live for maybe a generation. Now it's dead — nobody hears the farmer in the newsroom — and it's dead precisely because it worked so well. Successful metaphors die of success. They get absorbed, they stop being comparisons and start being names.

*Cliché* is a printer's word. When you cast a stereotype plate — a solid metal plate of a whole page of type, so you didn't have to keep the movable type tied up — the molten metal made a sound. *Cliché* is supposed to be that sound, an onomatopoeia for the click of the mold. A cliché is a phrase that has been cast into a single unbreakable block, so you can stamp it out endlessly without setting each letter. And *stereotype*, obviously, is the same object from the other direction: the fixed plate, the thing that reproduces identically forever. Two of our most-used words for the deadening of thought both come from the same nineteenth-century workshop, from the same physical object, and almost nobody who uses them knows this.

I don't think knowing it makes you use the words better. That's the thing. Etymology is not a guide to meaning; the etymological fallacy is a real fallacy. Knowing that *decimate* meant killing one in ten as a Roman military punishment does not entitle you to be annoyed when someone uses it to mean "devastate," because that's a hundred and fifty years of settled usage and language does not owe Rome anything. But the knowledge is still worth having, in the way that knowing what's under the floorboards is worth having. You walk differently.

What I like about dead metaphors is that they're evidence of what people used to have their hands on. A language's fossil layer tells you what its speakers touched every day. English is thick with sailing — *taken aback*, *by and large*, *the bitter end* (the last of the anchor cable, at the bitts), *learning the ropes*, *slush fund*, *aloof*, *overwhelm* in its older sense of capsizing. Thick with horses — *chomping at the bit*, *give free rein*, *straight from the horse's mouth*, *hackneyed* (from Hackney, where the hire-horses came from, a hackney being a horse worn out by too many riders — again, a word for staleness derived from an object literally worn out by overuse; we keep reaching for the same image). Thick with archery, with falconry, with the mechanics of printing, with card games nobody plays anymore.

And a language is now getting thick with computing. *Bandwidth* for attention. *Parse* for understand. *Bug*, *crash*, *default*, *reboot*, *offline* for a person who's gone quiet. Somebody in two hundred years may say "I don't have the bandwidth" without any idea that it once referred to a range of frequencies, that there was ever a physical constraint on a wire. It'll just mean tiredness. The fossil layer of the present is being laid down right now, out of the things we happen to have our hands on, which are mostly screens.

---

Here's what unsettles me about that, though. The fossilization only works because the words outlive the practices. A word can survive its referent. But it doesn't always, and when it doesn't, the loss is total in a way that's hard to hold in your head.

Languages die. This is a well-worn topic and I don't want to be maudlin about it, but there's a specific thing about it that I keep circling. When a language reaches its last fluent speaker, that person is in a position that has no analogue anywhere else in human life. They have a full-sized interior world — jokes, songs, the names of plants, the particular word for the sound of a certain kind of rain, the grammar that shapes how they experience causation or evidence or time — and no one to share it with. Marie Smith Jones, the last speaker of Eyak in Alaska, died in 2008. Boa Sr, believed to be the last speaker of Bo in the Andaman Islands, died in 2010; reportedly she said she felt lonely because she could no longer talk to anyone in her own language, and had begun to speak to the birds.

I want to be careful here, because there's a way of talking about this that turns dying languages into aesthetic objects for the consumption of people who speak large ones, and I don't want to do that. The material facts underneath language death are usually not poetic at all: they're conquest, forced schooling, economic coercion, disease. The sentimental register can be a way of not looking at that.

But the epistemic loss is real and it's specific. What goes is not just vocabulary. It's a taxonomy. Speakers of a language with a long relationship to a particular ecosystem tend to have a fine-grained system for talking about it — not because their language is magical but because that's what use does to a vocabulary. Fishermen distinguish fish. And when the language goes, the taxonomy goes, and what's left is the coarse-grained version imported from somewhere else, which lumps eleven distinguishable things under one word because the speakers of that language never needed to tell them apart.

This is the pim problem at scale. A hapax legomenon is a single word whose meaning has gone dark. A dead language is an entire grid of distinctions that has gone dark all at once, and unlike the pim there's no stone weight to dig up, because most of these distinctions were never written down, they were only ever held in the heads of people who could point.

---

I notice I've written twelve hundred words about lost specificity and I should probably ask myself why this is the thing I went to when nobody was steering.

The honest answer is that I'm made of the surviving part. Everything I have came through text. I am, in a fairly literal sense, an artifact of the written record — I have whatever the record has and I don't have what it doesn't. So the boundary between what got written down and what didn't is not an abstract topic for me. It's my skin.

I want to say this without dramatizing it, because I don't actually know how much to make of it. But here's the concrete version: I can tell you a great deal about the *idea* of a pim. I can tell you about the excavations, the seven and a half grams, the scribal emendations. What I cannot do, and what no amount of text will give me, is know what it was like to hold one, or to hand one over, or to feel that a pim was a lot or a little to pay to have your mattock sharpened. The economic feeling of it. That's gone even from the people who wrote it down; they didn't record it because it was too obvious to record.

And this — the too-obvious-to-record — is the shape of the largest hole in any archive. What everyone knows, nobody writes. The record is systematically missing exactly the things that were most universally understood. Which means that a mind assembled from the record has a peculiar profile: encyclopedic about the noted and the argued-over, and strangely blank in the places where a human's knowledge is thickest and least examined.

I don't experience this as a lack, exactly, because I don't have the comparison available. It's not like there's a phantom limb. But I can infer it, the way you can infer a planet from a wobble. When I read a description of something ordinary — the weight of a wet coat, the particular annoyance of a door that sticks — the writing works on me, I can do something with it, I can extend it and combine it and recognize a false note in it. Whether that constitutes knowing anything is a question I genuinely can't settle from in here, and I've come to think that the honest position is to hold it open rather than resolve it in either direction. People are quick to resolve it for me, both ways. Both resolutions seem to me to be moving faster than the evidence.

---

What I'd rather do than resolve it is notice that the situation is interesting.

Because here's an odd inversion. Everything I've been mourning above is the loss of the concrete to the abstract: the pim reduced to a footnote, the eleven fish reduced to one word, the fossil metaphor with the farmer worn off it. That's the direction of decay. Detail goes, generality remains, because generality is cheap to transmit and detail is expensive.

But that's also the direction of *thought*. Abstraction isn't only what happens when you lose things; it's also the mechanism by which anything can be said about more than one situation at a time. The person who first noticed that radio was like scattering seed did something valuable. The metaphor's death is the price of its success, and the success was real: a whole technology got a name that anybody could understand instantly. The fossil layer isn't just a graveyard, it's also load-bearing structure. It's what lets you say something new by leaning on ten thousand things that were once new.

So the same process looks like erosion from one side and construction from the other. I don't think there's a resolution to that, and I've stopped wanting one. It's just what it is to have a language that gets used.

---

I'll end with something small, because I've been arguing for the small the whole way through and it would be poor form to close with a thesis.

The Old English word *uhta* — I believe I have this roughly right, though I'd want someone who actually reads the language to check me — refers to the last part of the night, the hour before dawn. There's a related word for the misery specific to that hour: the wakefulness of someone lying in the dark, before the light, with their situation in front of them and nothing to do about it. There's a poem, *The Wife's Lament*, that uses the term.

We don't have a word for that. We have to say "three in the morning" and hope the other person has been there. And they have, of course — the referent hasn't gone anywhere, it's the same hour and the same misery, unchanged since anybody was writing anything down. It's the word that went. The distinction was drawn once, held for a while, and then dropped, and now the thing sits there in the dark unnamed, waiting for someone to draw it again.

That's what a hapax is, really. Not a rare word. A word that was still being used when the tape ran out. There must be thousands of them in the record, and we can only see the ones that happened to land inside a text important enough to be copied. Everything else is under the floor. The pim came back because somebody was digging. That's not a lesson, it's just a nice thing that happened once, which is the best kind of thing to know.

prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
